assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: CONJUNCTIVITIS, ORBITAL CELLULITIS (PRE-SEPTAL & SEPTAL)
---
Vomits everything is a danger sign and the eye swelling is severe in an under-5, so refer immediately.
Give cloxacillin 215 mg orally (25 mg/kg) or amoxycillin/clavulanate 215 mg orally now before the truck leaves.
If he vomits the medicine within 10 minutes, give the same dose again once.
Keep him on his side if vomiting, do not give food or drink by mouth if vomiting, keep warm.
Radio or phone the hospital: baby with orbital cellulitis, danger sign vomiting, antibiotic given, coming now. Note: age 10 months, weight 8.6 kg, eye swelling 2 days, vomiting everything, drug and time.

[guideline: BURNS AND SCALDS p27] CAUSES - A burn is usually caused by a hot object coming into contact with the skin - Chemicals such as acid can also cause burns - Hot liquids like boiling water often cause partial thickness burns or scalds MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT GOAL NOTES First aid Immediately immerse burn in cold running water for 20 mins This is to reduce serverity, still of use up to 3 hours after the burn Do not place ice directly on the burn Irrigate chemical burns with large volumes of cool clean water Assess burn area Using the picture diagram above Burns < 10% : Give extra fluid by mouth (e.g. water, coconut, ORS) Burns > 10%: Refer to hospital urgently as they require IV fluids Look for stridor Or hoarse voice - this indicates upper airway inflammation Risk particularly in neck/facial burns Give pain relief Regular paracetamol and consider morphine (0.1mg/kg per bolus) Clean & dress burn Clean and debride away dirt or dead tissue with antiseptic solution/salt water Apply silver sulphadiazine (SSD) cream or any antiseptic cream daily Fluids - 1st Day: Give an extra 4ml/kg for every 1% of area burnt PLUS maintenance fluids 1/2 of this extra fluid is given over 8 hours & remaining 1/2 over the next 16 hours Fluids - 2nd Day Give 3/4 of the total fluids required in the first day Give antibiotics If the burn looks infected Cloxacillin IV/oral depending on severity Monitor for sepsis Consider tetanus First check tetanus status Give if not fully immunised, >5 yrs since last tetanus or uncertain history ...

Keep the leg clean: wash with salt water or antiseptic, take away dead skin, then put SSD cream or antiseptic cream.
The burn looks infected so give cloxacillin. For 6.2 kg, 50 mg/kg = 310 mg orally, and continue as the manual says.
Pain relief: paracetamol 6.2 kg x 15 mg = about 93 mg orally every 6 hours.
Check tetanus status. If not fully immunised or unsure, give tetanus now.
Referral note: age, weight, scald on leg, signs of infection, cloxacillin and paracetamol given, tetanus status, time sent.

[guideline: RHEUMATIC FEVER p90] Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) is a common cause of acquired childhood heart disease in Solomon Islands, most common in 5 - 14 year old children. The illness caused by a reaction to a bacterial infection (Group A streptococcus, GAS) which usually begins in the throat or potentially on the skin. ARF causes inflammation in joints and damage to the heart valves which can be permanent and is known as Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) If child is unwell and suspect ARF, refer to the nearest hospital for investigations and treatment. For further guidance please refer to the WHO Pocketbook of Hospital Care for children (2 nd Edition, 2013) and the Solomon Islands Protocol on Rheumatic Heart Disease

Also advise that conjuctivitis is contagious and to always wash hands with soap and water before and after touching the eye - If conjunctivitis fails to respond to initial treatment or is associated with more severe symptoms such as significant pain, loss of vision or photophobia treat as severe conjunctivitis and refer. - Severe bacterial conjuctivitis (a lot of pus or redness or swelling of the eyelids) - Topical antibiotics alone are insufficient - Give cefotaxime 100 mg/kg IV or IM as a single dose OR - Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (maximum 1 gram) IV or IM as a single dose - If ceftriaxone/cefotaxime unavailable, use IM Benzylpenicillin 60mg/kg IV/IM every 8 hours for 5 days - Severe conjunctivitis in a neonate (in the first 5 days of life) may be due to a STI - In neonates <1 month ...

They can also lead to serious infections of the blood. Also consider non-infectious causes of skin disease (e.g. eczema, allergies). PREVENTION OF SKIN DISEASES Skin diseases can often be prevented by good skin hygiene and use of soap and water Advise parents - Keep skin clean. Wash with soap and water daily, drying well between fingers and toes - Do not share towels between infected children - Get treatment for small skin sores early before they get big - Use of medicated soaps may prevent small skin sores becoming serious Prevention of spreading infection and re-infection - Many skin diseases are contagious. Always treat other infected family members or contacts at the same time.

[guideline: RHEUMATIC FEVER p90] Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) is a common cause of acquired childhood heart disease in Solomon Islands, most common in 5 - 14 year old children. Always calculate on the amount of elemental iron in the mixture For Ferrous mixture 20mg/1ml (contains 6mg of elemental iron in 1ml): WEIGHT (kg) MIXTURE 3 - 5.9 6 - 9.9 10 - 14.9 15 - 19.9 20mg/ml 1ml 2.5ml 4ml 5ml - Plan to continue oral iron replacement for 3 months, recheck Hb o If no improvement, firstly check compliance with medication o Consider increasing dose o Consider alternative diagnosis (e.g chronic infection or disease) - If the child cannot take oral iron, consider IM injection. Discuss with paediatrician.

[guideline: RHEUMATIC FEVER p90] SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Signs of acute rheumatic fever: see Jones criteria above - Signs of chronic rheumatic fever. Heart damage already done from this episode (late presentation) or previous episodes of rheumatic fever - Heart murmur - Heart failure (enlarged liver, tachycardia, lung crepitations) - Signs of infective endocarditis (a serious complication of RHD, can be acute or chronic) INVESTIGATIONS - Bloods: o FBE, ESR/CRP if available o Blood cultures if febrile (multiple if concerns of infective endocarditis) o Streptococcal serology: ASO and anti-DNase B titres - Can be normal early in the illness. Confirm by rising titres 2 weeks later - Other: o Throat swab for GAS culture: preferably before giving antibiotics o ECG: looking for elevated PR interval, abnormal rhythm o CXR: looking for evidence of an enlarged heart or heart failure o Echocardiogram (if available): to confirm carditis and exclude infective endocarditis o Consider joint aspirate if concerns of septic arthritis as a differential

[guideline: BURNS AND SCALDS p27] CAUSES - A burn is usually caused by a hot object coming into contact with the skin - Chemicals such as acid can also cause burns - Hot liquids like boiling water often cause partial thickness burns or scalds MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT GOAL NOTES First aid Immediately immerse burn in cold running water for 20 mins This is to reduce serverity, still of use up to 3 hours after the burn Do not place ice directly on the burn Irrigate chemical burns with large volumes of cool clean water Assess burn area Using the picture diagram above Burns < 10% : Give extra fluid by mouth (e.g. water, coconut, ORS) Burns > 10%: Refer to hospital urgently as they require IV fluids Look for stridor Or hoarse voice - this indicates upper airway inflammation Risk particularly in neck/facial burns Give pain relief Regular paracetamol and consider morphine (0.1mg/kg per bolus) Clean & dress burn Clean and debride away dirt or dead tissue with antiseptic solution/salt water Apply silver sulphadiazine (SSD) cream or any antiseptic cream daily Fluids - 1st Day: Give an extra 4ml/kg for every 1% of area burnt PLUS maintenance fluids 1/2 of this extra fluid is given over 8 hours & remaining 1/2 over the next 16 hours Fluids - 2nd Day Give 3/4 of the total fluids required in the first day Give antibiotics If the burn looks infected Cloxacillin IV/oral depending on severity Monitor for sepsis Consider tetanus First check tetanus status Give if not fully immunised, >5 yrs since last tetanus or uncertain history ...

Kambak kwiktaem sapos hem toraot evri samting, no fit dring, skin blong hem kol an blu, o burn hem kam moa big.
Kambak long 2 dei fo lukim burn, o kwiktaem sapos hem hot bodi o pus.

[guideline: ANAEMIA p18] Treatment of anaemia - Consider malaria treatment and give hookworm treatment with albendazole - Give advice on good nutrition o Diet rich in meat, fish, chicken, peanuts, green leafy vegetables, beans, lentils o Eating raw, washed vegetables and fruit (such as paw-paw, mango, pineapple and orange) helps the body to absorb iron - Give iron treatment (calculate doses carefully as Iron is toxic on overdose) o Re-check Hb after 4 weeks o Should be given orally if possible - Dose: 2 - 6 mg/kg/day elemental iron (max 200mg) - There are different formulations available for iron. Always calculate on the amount of elemental iron in the mixture For Ferrous mixture 20mg/1ml (contains 6mg of elemental iron in 1ml): WEIGHT (kg) MIXTURE 3 - 5.9 6 - 9.9 10 - 14.9 15 - 19.9 20mg/ml 1ml 2.5ml 4ml 5ml - Plan to continue oral iron replacement for 3 months, recheck Hb o If no improvement, firstly check compliance with medication o Consider increasing dose o Consider alternative diagnosis (e.g chronic infection or disease) - If the child cannot take oral iron, consider IM injection. Discuss with paediatrician.
Boy 4 years old, about 15.5 kg. He is very tired, and when I look his palms and the inside of his eyes they are white, not pink. He cannot walk to the clinic door by himself. The truck is here now and can take him straight away.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: ANAEMIA
---
This is severe anaemia: pale palms and conjunctiva with tiredness. Send him to hospital now in the truck.
Before he goes, take blood for Hb and do a malaria test if you have a kit.
If you have artemether-lumefantrine, give 2 tablets now with milk or fatty food, and start iron 2 mg/kg = 31 mg elemental iron by mouth if he can swallow.
Keep him warm, lying flat, and let him sip water or breastfeed on the way.
Call the hospital or AHC by phone or radio to say he is coming.
Write the referral note: age, weight, pale palms, Hb if known, malaria test result, drugs and times given.

Show the carer as you do this: o Use a piece of toilet tissue, twist lightly from one corner to form a tissue spear o Tear off the tip at each end o Get carer to steady the child's head while you pull the top ...

[guideline: GLOMERULONEPHRITIS p41] CAUSES - Inflammation of the kidney - A common cause is Acute Post Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN). o Usually follows a streptococcal skin or throat infection by 2 - 4 weeks INVESTIGATION - Urine dipstick and microscopy (looking for protein and red cells) - Renal function and electrolytes - Consider ASOT, Anti-DNAse - Consider renal ultrasound MANAGEMENT - Admit and refer the child - Monitor urine output and asses fluid clinically overloaded - If poor urine output, assess hydration - If dehydration, carefully rehydrate - If signs of clinical overload then consider fluid restriction (1/2 maintenance) & frusemide 0.5-1mg/kg IV/PO - Treat hypertension (refer to age-appropriate reference graphs): - Nifedipine - If child < 2 years give 2.5mg every 12 hours - If child > 2 years give 5mg every 12 hours OR - Enalapril - 0.1mg/kg/day in 1 or 2 doses gradually increasing to max 1mg/kg/day (usual adult dose 20mg to 40mg per day) - Give benzathine penicillin IM as single dose to treat any underlying streptococcal infection: - Child weighs <20kg give 450mg (0.6 mega units) - Child weighs <20kg give 900mg (1.2 mega units)
Pikinini 3 yia haf, 15 kilo. Hem garem skin sores long leg finis 3 wik, nau face blong hem puffy an urine blong hem dark olsem kola. Hem no garem sek-sek, hem dring gud. No transport i stap, ples blong mifala longwe.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: GLOMERULONEPHRITIS
---
Diswan luk olsem glomerulonephritis: puffy face an dark kola urine afta skin sores. Hem mas go long hospital.

Givim benzathine penicillin IM wan taem nomoa: 900 mg (1.2 mega units) from hem 15 kg.
Lukluk urine output an sapos face hem puffy moa o hem brit had, talem dokta long fon.
Raetem referral leta: skin sores 3 wik, puffy face, dark urine, weight, penicillin dose an taem.

[guideline: OSTEOMYELITIS, SEPTIC ARTHRITIS, PYOMYOSITIS p77] - Osteomyelitis is infection of the bone - Septic arthritis is infection of a joint - Pyomyositis is infection of the muscle with pus present. - These are serious infections as they may cause permanent damage and impairment in mobility SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever, usually intermittent - Warm, painful, swollen joint (septic arthritis) or limb/back(osteomyelitis/pyomyositis) o Pyomyositis commonly involves the thigh - Irritability in neonate or infant - Inability or refusal to move a limb/joint or to walk (in mobile child) - Skin abscess/sinus draining from chronic underlying osteomyelitis CAUSES - Bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) - May be secondary to trauma or spread through the bloodstream from another site of infection (e.g: cellulitis, respiratory tract) INVESTIGATION - X-ray of bone and joint associated joint space. In early osteomyelitis, the x-ray may be normal as it takes up to 2 weeks for changes to be seen - If associated skin wound/abscess, a culture of pus from wound - Full blood count & blood culture, ESR MANAGEMENT - Referal to Orthopedic Team (osteomyelitis, septic arthritis) or General Sugical team (pyomyositis) for consideration of surgery - Septic arthritis requires urgent surgical drainage & joint lavage. This needs to be done as soon as possible to reduce the risk of permanent joint destruction - Pyomyositis usually needs incision and drainage of abscess - Chronic osteomyelitis may require sequestrectomy (removal of dead bone)

[guideline: BURNS AND SCALDS p27] CAUSES - A burn is usually caused by a hot object coming into contact with the skin - Chemicals such as acid can also cause burns - Hot liquids like boiling water often cause partial thickness burns or scalds MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT GOAL NOTES First aid Immediately immerse burn in cold running water for 20 mins This is to reduce serverity, still of use up to 3 hours after the burn Do not place ice directly on the burn Irrigate chemical burns with large volumes of cool clean water Assess burn area Using the picture diagram above Burns < 10% : Give extra fluid by mouth (e.g. water, coconut, ORS) Burns > 10%: Refer to hospital urgently as they require IV fluids Look for stridor Or hoarse voice - this indicates upper airway inflammation Risk particularly in neck/facial burns Give pain relief Regular paracetamol and consider morphine (0.1mg/kg per bolus) Clean & dress burn Clean and debride away dirt or dead tissue with antiseptic solution/salt water Apply silver sulphadiazine (SSD) cream or any antiseptic cream daily Fluids - 1st Day: Give an extra 4ml/kg for every 1% of area burnt PLUS maintenance fluids 1/2 of this extra fluid is given over 8 hours & remaining 1/2 over the next 16 hours Fluids - 2nd Day Give 3/4 of the total fluids required in the first day Give antibiotics If the burn looks infected Cloxacillin IV/oral depending on severity Monitor for sepsis Consider tetanus First check tetanus status Give if not fully immunised, >5 yrs since last tetanus or uncertain history ...
Fourteen month old, about 10.1 kg. Hot water splashed on her lower leg this afternoon, small scald, skin is red with one small blister. She is alert, drinking and no breathing problem. Next boat is tomorrow. What do I do and when do I see her again?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: BURNS AND SCALDS
---
The area is small, under 10 percent, but send her on tomorrow's boat so the burn can be checked and dressed properly.
Tonight put the leg in clean running water for 20 minutes, do not put ice.
Give extra fluids by mouth, water or ORS, 4 ml for each 1 percent of burn plus her normal feeds.
Paracetamol 150 mg (15 mg/kg) every 6 hours for pain.
Clean with salt water, apply silver sulphadiazine cream, cover with a clean dressing, and check tetanus.
Send her sooner by radio if she gets fever, the burn smells or weeps pus, or her voice becomes hoarse.

[guideline: RHEUMATIC FEVER p90] Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) is a common cause of acquired childhood heart disease in Solomon Islands, most common in 5 - 14 year old children. The illness caused by a reaction to a bacterial infection (Group A streptococcus, GAS) which usually begins in the throat or potentially on the skin. ARF causes inflammation in joints and damage to the heart valves which can be permanent and is known as Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) If child is unwell and suspect ARF, refer to the nearest hospital for investigations and treatment. For further guidance please refer to the WHO Pocketbook of Hospital Care for children (2 nd Edition, 2013) and the Solomon Islands Protocol on Rheumatic Heart Disease

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES- JAUNDICE p72] Jaundice is yellow colouring of the skin and eyes. It is caused by bilirubin, which is formed when red blood cells (haemoglobin) are broken down. Many babies have jaundice, which is normal and requires no treatment. Abnormal Jaundice, which requires treatment includes - Jaundice on the first day of life - Jaundice lasting longer than 14 days - Jaundice with fever - Babies with severe jaundice; palms and soles deeply yellow Signs & Symptoms - Yellow colouring of skin, palms, soles, eyes (In normal jaundice, often only the skin and eyes are slightly yellow) - Signs of infection (fever, baby looks unwell, not feeding; 62) - Signs of anaemia (due to haemolysis) Causes - Serious infection (bacterial, syphilis, malaria) - Haemolysis due to ABO incompatibility or G6PD deficiency (early onset jaundice) - Physiological jaundice (from day 3-4) - Prematurity - Hypothyroidism and other metabolic disorders - Liver disease such as biliary atresia - Jaundice is also made worse if the neonate is dehydrated

[guideline: OSTEOMYELITIS, SEPTIC ARTHRITIS, PYOMYOSITIS p77] - Osteomyelitis is infection of the bone - Septic arthritis is infection of a joint - Pyomyositis is infection of the muscle with pus present. - These are serious infections as they may cause permanent damage and impairment in mobility SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever, usually intermittent - Warm, painful, swollen joint (septic arthritis) or limb/back(osteomyelitis/pyomyositis) o Pyomyositis commonly involves the thigh - Irritability in neonate or infant - Inability or refusal to move a limb/joint or to walk (in mobile child) - Skin abscess/sinus draining from chronic underlying osteomyelitis CAUSES - Bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) - May be secondary to trauma or spread through the bloodstream from another site of infection (e.g: cellulitis, respiratory tract) INVESTIGATION - X-ray of bone and joint associated joint space. In early osteomyelitis, the x-ray may be normal as it takes up to 2 weeks for changes to be seen - If associated skin wound/abscess, a culture of pus from wound - Full blood count & blood culture, ESR MANAGEMENT - Referal to Orthopedic Team (osteomyelitis, septic arthritis) or General Sugical team (pyomyositis) for consideration of surgery - Septic arthritis requires urgent surgical drainage & joint lavage. This needs to be done as soon as possible to reduce the risk of permanent joint destruction - Pyomyositis usually needs incision and drainage of abscess - Chronic osteomyelitis may require sequestrectomy (removal of dead bone)

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES- JAUNDICE p72] Jaundice is yellow colouring of the skin and eyes. It is caused by bilirubin, which is formed when red blood cells (haemoglobin) are broken down. Many babies have jaundice, which is normal and requires no treatment. Abnormal Jaundice, which requires treatment includes - Jaundice on the first day of life - Jaundice lasting longer than 14 days - Jaundice with fever - Babies with severe jaundice; palms and soles deeply yellow Signs & Symptoms - Yellow colouring of skin, palms, soles, eyes (In normal jaundice, often only the skin and eyes are slightly yellow) - Signs of infection (fever, baby looks unwell, not feeding; 62) - Signs of anaemia (due to haemolysis) Causes - Serious infection (bacterial, syphilis, malaria) - Haemolysis due to ABO incompatibility or G6PD deficiency (early onset jaundice) - Physiological jaundice (from day 3-4) - Prematurity - Hypothyroidism and other metabolic disorders - Liver disease such as biliary atresia - Jaundice is also made worse if the neonate is dehydrated

[guideline: SURGICAL PROBLEMS p100] A child with a tender, swollen scrotum or tender, distended abdomen or bile stained vomiting should be referred urgently to hospital SCROTAL SWELLINGS There are several causes for swelling in the scrotum. The most common ones include - Hydrocele (collection of fluid around the testicle) - Hernia (loop of bowel entering the scrotum) - Testicular torsion - Epididymo-orchitis Hydrocele - A common cause of swelling in the scrotum and is the result of fluid building up around the testicle. It usually has been there for a long time - The child is well, feeds well and the scrotum is not painful to touch - It is usually possible to feel a normal cord above the swelling - The swelling is soft. When a torch is placed against it, it transilluminates (lights up) very brightly - Hydroceles usually get better by themselves. If there is any doubt about the diagnosis or the child is older than 2 years, the child should be referred to the Surgical Team Hernia (Inguinal) - A hernia is caused when the opening to the scrotum is bigger than normal and a loop of bowel enters into the scrotum. - Sometimes the loop of bowel slides in and out of the scrotum so that the swelling is only there sometimes (a reducible inguninal hernia). In this case the swelling can usually be pushed gently up and out of the scrotum and the scrotum is a normal colour. o These children should be referred to a surgeon - In some children, the loop of bowel becomes stuck (non-reducible), causing a tender, swollen, sometimes discoloured scrotum ...
Mere blong pikinini 84 manis, 23.6 kilo, i kolsap long klinik. Skrotum blong hem swol an hat, no pushum bek. Bel bikfala, no pass stool from yestedei. Hemi hot bodi smol. RDT positive, ACT iumi garem. Taem fo go hospital naoia.
assistant:

Givim paracetamol 15 mg fo evri kilo (354 mg) fo pen. Start IV saline 20 ml/kg (472 ml) bolus.
No givim ACT malaria taem diswan. Diswan surgical emergence, no malaria problem nomoa.
Putum NG tube, no kaikai o dring, kipim pikinini warm an putum long said.
Sendem go kwiktaem wetem leta: 7 yia, 23.6 kg, suspect strangulated hernia, RDT positive incidental.

[guideline: OSTEOMYELITIS, SEPTIC ARTHRITIS, PYOMYOSITIS p77] - Osteomyelitis is infection of the bone - Septic arthritis is infection of a joint - Pyomyositis is infection of the muscle with pus present. - These are serious infections as they may cause permanent damage and impairment in mobility SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever, usually intermittent - Warm, painful, swollen joint (septic arthritis) or limb/back(osteomyelitis/pyomyositis) o Pyomyositis commonly involves the thigh - Irritability in neonate or infant - Inability or refusal to move a limb/joint or to walk (in mobile child) - Skin abscess/sinus draining from chronic underlying osteomyelitis CAUSES - Bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) - May be secondary to trauma or spread through the bloodstream from another site of infection (e.g: cellulitis, respiratory tract) INVESTIGATION - X-ray of bone and joint associated joint space. In early osteomyelitis, the x-ray may be normal as it takes up to 2 weeks for changes to be seen - If associated skin wound/abscess, a culture of pus from wound - Full blood count & blood culture, ESR MANAGEMENT - Referal to Orthopedic Team (osteomyelitis, septic arthritis) or General Sugical team (pyomyositis) for consideration of surgery - Septic arthritis requires urgent surgical drainage & joint lavage. This needs to be done as soon as possible to reduce the risk of permanent joint destruction - Pyomyositis usually needs incision and drainage of abscess - Chronic osteomyelitis may require sequestrectomy (removal of dead bone)

[guideline: SURGICAL PROBLEMS p100] A child with a tender, swollen scrotum or tender, distended abdomen or bile stained vomiting should be referred urgently to hospital SCROTAL SWELLINGS There are several causes for swelling in the scrotum. The most common ones include - Hydrocele (collection of fluid around the testicle) - Hernia (loop of bowel entering the scrotum) - Testicular torsion - Epididymo-orchitis Hydrocele - A common cause of swelling in the scrotum and is the result of fluid building up around the testicle. It usually has been there for a long time - The child is well, feeds well and the scrotum is not painful to touch - It is usually possible to feel a normal cord above the swelling - The swelling is soft. When a torch is placed against it, it transilluminates (lights up) very brightly - Hydroceles usually get better by themselves. If there is any doubt about the diagnosis or the child is older than 2 years, the child should be referred to the Surgical Team Hernia (Inguinal) - A hernia is caused when the opening to the scrotum is bigger than normal and a loop of bowel enters into the scrotum. - Sometimes the loop of bowel slides in and out of the scrotum so that the swelling is only there sometimes (a reducible inguninal hernia). In this case the swelling can usually be pushed gently up and out of the scrotum and the scrotum is a normal colour. o These children should be referred to a surgeon - In some children, the loop of bowel becomes stuck (non-reducible), causing a tender, swollen, sometimes discoloured scrotum ...

[guideline: RHEUMATIC FEVER p90] SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Signs of acute rheumatic fever: see Jones criteria above - Signs of chronic rheumatic fever. Heart damage already done from this episode (late presentation) or previous episodes of rheumatic fever - Heart murmur - Heart failure (enlarged liver, tachycardia, lung crepitations) - Signs of infective endocarditis (a serious complication of RHD, can be acute or chronic) INVESTIGATIONS - Bloods: o FBE, ESR/CRP if available o Blood cultures if febrile (multiple if concerns of infective endocarditis) o Streptococcal serology: ASO and anti-DNase B titres - Can be normal early in the illness. Confirm by rising titres 2 weeks later - Other: o Throat swab for GAS culture: preferably before giving antibiotics o ECG: looking for elevated PR interval, abnormal rhythm o CXR: looking for evidence of an enlarged heart or heart failure o Echocardiogram (if available): to confirm carditis and exclude infective endocarditis o Consider joint aspirate if concerns of septic arthritis as a differential
Girl 10 years old, weight around 34 kg. Two weeks ago she had a very sore throat that we did not treat. Now both knees and her right wrist are swollen and very painful, she does not want to walk. I listened to her heart and I can hear a murmur. No fever today. What should I do for her?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: RHEUMATIC FEVER
---
This fits acute rheumatic fever: sore throat, then painful swollen joints, and now a heart murmur. She needs referral for tests you cannot do here.
Check now for heart failure: fast pulse, big liver, crackles in the lungs, and any fever that may mean infective endocarditis.
Take blood for FBE and ESR/CRP if you can, do a throat swab before any antibiotic, and do an ECG and CXR if available.
Give paracetamol for the joint pain and keep her resting quietly until the boat or truck comes.
Refer her to hospital for echocardiogram and streptococcal serology (ASO, anti-DNase B), and send a note of all findings.
Come back sooner if she cannot lie flat, breathes fast, or the joints get worse.

[guideline: ANAEMIA p18] Treatment of anaemia - Consider malaria treatment and give hookworm treatment with albendazole - Give advice on good nutrition o Diet rich in meat, fish, chicken, peanuts, green leafy vegetables, beans, lentils o Eating raw, washed vegetables and fruit (such as paw-paw, mango, pineapple and orange) helps the body to absorb iron - Give iron treatment (calculate doses carefully as Iron is toxic on overdose) o Re-check Hb after 4 weeks o Should be given orally if possible - Dose: 2 - 6 mg/kg/day elemental iron (max 200mg) - There are different formulations available for iron. Always calculate on the amount of elemental iron in the mixture For Ferrous mixture 20mg/1ml (contains 6mg of elemental iron in 1ml): WEIGHT (kg) MIXTURE 3 - 5.9 6 - 9.9 10 - 14.9 15 - 19.9 20mg/ml 1ml 2.5ml 4ml 5ml - Plan to continue oral iron replacement for 3 months, recheck Hb o If no improvement, firstly check compliance with medication o Consider increasing dose o Consider alternative diagnosis (e.g chronic infection or disease) - If the child cannot take oral iron, consider IM injection. Discuss with paediatrician.
Mama bring pikinini 2 yia olsem, weight 12 kilo 500 gram. Hemi pale long hem face an hand, hem tired tumas. No malaria test here, no boat today. What medicine I give him?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: ANAEMIA
---
Check for danger signs: if he cannot drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, has convulsions, is very sleepy, or has fast breathing with chest indrawing, call the AHC by radio for urgent referral.
Give iron mixture 4 ml once daily (contains 24 mg elemental iron, 2 mg/kg/day). Continue for 3 months and recheck Hb in 4 weeks.
Give albendazole for hookworm treatment.
Advise mama: give meat, fish, chicken, peanuts, green leaf vegetables, beans; raw washed paw-paw, mango, pineapple, orange helps iron absorption.
Since no RDT, do malaria test when available and treat if positive. Come back in 4 weeks or sooner if he looks worse.

[guideline: RHEUMATIC FEVER p90] Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) is a common cause of acquired childhood heart disease in Solomon Islands, most common in 5 - 14 year old children. The illness caused by a reaction to a bacterial infection (Group A streptococcus, GAS) which usually begins in the throat or potentially on the skin. ARF causes inflammation in joints and damage to the heart valves which can be permanent and is known as Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) If child is unwell and suspect ARF, refer to the nearest hospital for investigations and treatment. For further guidance please refer to the WHO Pocketbook of Hospital Care for children (2 nd Edition, 2013) and the Solomon Islands Protocol on Rheumatic Heart Disease

[guideline: OSTEOMYELITIS, SEPTIC ARTHRITIS, PYOMYOSITIS p77] - Osteomyelitis is infection of the bone - Septic arthritis is infection of a joint - Pyomyositis is infection of the muscle with pus present. - These are serious infections as they may cause permanent damage and impairment in mobility SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever, usually intermittent - Warm, painful, swollen joint (septic arthritis) or limb/back(osteomyelitis/pyomyositis) o Pyomyositis commonly involves the thigh - Irritability in neonate or infant - Inability or refusal to move a limb/joint or to walk (in mobile child) - Skin abscess/sinus draining from chronic underlying osteomyelitis CAUSES - Bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) - May be secondary to trauma or spread through the bloodstream from another site of infection (e.g: cellulitis, respiratory tract) INVESTIGATION - X-ray of bone and joint associated joint space. In early osteomyelitis, the x-ray may be normal as it takes up to 2 weeks for changes to be seen - If associated skin wound/abscess, a culture of pus from wound - Full blood count & blood culture, ESR MANAGEMENT - Referal to Orthopedic Team (osteomyelitis, septic arthritis) or General Sugical team (pyomyositis) for consideration of surgery - Septic arthritis requires urgent surgical drainage & joint lavage. This needs to be done as soon as possible to reduce the risk of permanent joint destruction - Pyomyositis usually needs incision and drainage of abscess - Chronic osteomyelitis may require sequestrectomy (removal of dead bone)

[guideline: SURGICAL PROBLEMS p100] A child with a tender, swollen scrotum or tender, distended abdomen or bile stained vomiting should be referred urgently to hospital SCROTAL SWELLINGS There are several causes for swelling in the scrotum. The most common ones include - Hydrocele (collection of fluid around the testicle) - Hernia (loop of bowel entering the scrotum) - Testicular torsion - Epididymo-orchitis Hydrocele - A common cause of swelling in the scrotum and is the result of fluid building up around the testicle. It usually has been there for a long time - The child is well, feeds well and the scrotum is not painful to touch - It is usually possible to feel a normal cord above the swelling - The swelling is soft. When a torch is placed against it, it transilluminates (lights up) very brightly - Hydroceles usually get better by themselves. If there is any doubt about the diagnosis or the child is older than 2 years, the child should be referred to the Surgical Team Hernia (Inguinal) - A hernia is caused when the opening to the scrotum is bigger than normal and a loop of bowel enters into the scrotum. - Sometimes the loop of bowel slides in and out of the scrotum so that the swelling is only there sometimes (a reducible inguninal hernia). In this case the swelling can usually be pushed gently up and out of the scrotum and the scrotum is a normal colour. o These children should be referred to a surgeon - In some children, the loop of bowel becomes stuck (non-reducible), causing a tender, swollen, sometimes discoloured scrotum ...

assistant:

Send her on the next boat tomorrow morning, but start treatment here tonight.
Cool the burn with clean running water for 20 minutes, do not use ice.
Give extra fluids by mouth: breastfeed often plus water or ORS, about 4 ml for each 1 percent of burn plus her normal feeds.
Paracetamol 120 mg (15 mg/kg) every 6 hours for pain, and morphine 0.8 mg per bolus if the pain is very bad.
Clean and dress with silver sulphadiazine cream daily, check tetanus and give it if she is not immunised.
If her voice goes hoarse or she breathes hard, that is the airway, send her at once by radio, do not wait for the boat.

[guideline: MALARIA p53] INVESTIGATION - Malaria slide (MPS) OR Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) - Blood glucose MANAGEMENT - Consider malaria in any child with a fever. Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria
Baby 4 months, around 6 kg. Mother says he had fever since yesterday, now he is very sleepy and hard to wake, and his body looks yellow. The boat to town leaves tomorrow morning, no other transport.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: MALARIA
---
This is severe malaria: jaundice and lethargy are danger signs. Baby must go to hospital on tomorrow's boat.
While you wait: treat for severe malaria. Give artesunate 14.4 mg (2.4 mg per kg) IM now, repeat at 12 hours, then daily. If no artesunate IM, put artesunate 60 mg rectally (10 mg per kg).

[guideline: PERTUSSIS (WHOOPING COUGH) p81] Whooping cough occurs when the bacteria Bordetella pertussis gets into the respiratory tract and causes a bloody mucous to be formed CAUSE - Spread by air droplets - Patients are contagious for 21 days after the onset of the cough, if untreated - Non-vaccinated children most commonly affected. Can occur in immunised children but usually a more mild illness SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Cough and runny nose for 1 week (1st stage) followed by spasmodic cough with 'whooping' sound. May also present as a non-specific persistant cough - Vomiting often following a coughing spasm - Apnoea or cyanosis during coughing spasms - Fever is uncommon - There may be no clinical signs on examination and children may appear well between coughing spasms COMPLICATIONS - Infants < 6 months are at greatest risk and are commonly infected by family members - Apnoea - Severe pneumonia - Encephalopathy INVESTIGATIONS - Generally a clinical diagnosis - If persistant cough or other suggestive symptoms (weight loss, night sweats) remember to assess TB exposure and consider investigations if risk factors - Blood count (may be associated with high lymphocyte count) MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT NOTES:
Bebi 12 month, 9.3 kilo. Hem garem wheeze an hem no save tok gud, brit blong hem hariap an chest go insaet. Bot i kam next boat. Wanem nao mi mas duim?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: ASTHMA
---
Pikinini garem saen blong denja: no save tok, brit hariap tumas, chest indrawing.
Givim oxygen sapos i stap, putum hem long sidaon posisin.
Sapos salbutamol inhaler i stap, givim 4 puff wetem spacer evri 20 minit taem yu wetem bot.
Kolemem AHC long radio fo talem hem i kam.
Sendem hem go long hospital long fes bot.
No givim kaikai taem hem no save swallo gud.

[guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] PROMOTE BREAST FEEDING - It is safe, simple, readily available and cheap - It contains all the nutrients that the baby needs to grow - It reduces the risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition and other diseases - Helps encourage bonding between mother and baby FACTS ABOUT BREAST FEEDING - Breast feeding should begin within the first hour after delivery - The first yellow milk a mother makes (colostrum) should be given to the baby. o It should not be thrown away as it contains important immunoglobulins that are part of the baby's defense against infection - The easiest and best schedule is 'on-demand' breast feeding o Infants who cannot demand feed (such as low birth weight or sick babies) should be fed every 2-3 hours o Infants who cannot suck on the breast (eg. very premature babies) should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup/spoon or by NG tube - Ideally all babies should be exclusively breast fed for the first 6 months o Solids should be introduced from 6 months o Cow's milk or powdered milk should be avoided before the age of 12 months because of the risk of iron-deficiency anaemia - Breast feeding should continue for as long as possible. - Breast feeding policies should be supported and upheld always - Bottles with teats and baby cups with spouts should discouraged. o They are difficult to sterilize and may result in infections such as diarrhoea - For facts about breast feeding in HIV positive mothers

[guideline: CONVULSIONS p34] ONGOING SEIZURE CONTROL Children with epilepsy usually require maintenance anticonvulsants MEDICATION DOSAGE If less than 3 yrs: Phenobarbitone 2.5- 5mg/kg/day in 1 or 2 doses (max 240mg per day) Use: Generalised or partial seizures Phenytoin 2-4mg/kg/day every 12 hours (max 300mg per day) Not for use during pregnancy If more than 3 yrs: Sodium Valproate 5mg/kg every 12 hours up to max 20 mg/kg (max 2g) every 12 hours Use: all types of epilepsy (generalised, partial, absence) Carbamazepine 2.5mg/kg every 12 hours, can increase over 2-4 weeks to 10mg/kg (max 500mg) every 12 hours Use: Generalised, partial seizures
Girl 3 and a half years, 14.6 kg, one short fit at home this morning with hot body, awake now and playing. No RDT in the clinic, not sure about ACT. No boat today. Write a short message for the mother.
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: CONVULSIONS
---
Give carbamazepine 37 mg by mouth every 12 hours (2.5 mg/kg, child is over 3 years).
Give paracetamol for the fever and keep her drinking and eating.
Keep her away from the fire and the sea until the fits are controlled.
Come back at once if a fit lasts more than 5 minutes, she is hard to wake, vomits everything, or her neck is stiff.
Review at the clinic in 2 weeks, and sooner if she fits again.

[guideline: FEVER p40] - Fever is defined as an axillary (under the arm) temperature greater than 37.5 oC - Fever in itself is not dangerous as it helps the body to fight infection CAUSES The common causes of fever in children are: - Common viral infections: upper respiratory tract infection, measles, gastroenteritis - Common bacterial: pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, urinary tract infections - Other: Malaria, tuberculosis INVESTIGATIONS - Consider blood film or rapid diagnostic test for malaria parasites - If possible, collect and test a urine sample MANAGEMENT - Treat the cause of the fever - Consider antimalarials - Consider giving paracetamol if fever above 38ºC AND the child is irritable o Dose: 15mg/kg (max 1g) every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 doses in 24 hours) o Do not use aspirin in children for fever - Give extra fluids Consider the following causes for fever greater than 7 days: - Abscess - Salmonella infection - Infective endocarditis - Rheumatic fever - Tuberculosis Fever helps the body to fight infection Try to find and treat the cause of the fever
Girl 4 and a half years, around 16 kg. Fever started Monday, she is grumpy and only picks at her food. She is drinking well, no vomiting, no fits. We have no RDT kits left in the clinic but we do have ACT. What should I do for her?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: FEVER
---
No danger signs here, so this can be managed at the clinic.
Check her temperature and look for the cause: ears, throat, chest, urine.
No malaria test today, so if she has no other cause and fever keeps on, treat as malaria with ACT per the manual.
If her temperature is above 38 and she is irritable, give paracetamol 246 mg (15 mg/kg) every 4 to 6 hours, no more than 4 doses in 24 hours.
Do not give aspirin. Give extra fluids and keep her eating small amounts often.
Come back in 2 days, or sooner if she cannot drink, vomits everything, fits, or becomes sleepy.

10 month old, 9.8 kg, has had two fits today and is still twitching now. No malaria test kit here but we have ACT. Boat goes tomorrow. What should I give while we wait?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: CONVULSIONS
---
Ongoing fits need urgent referral - send on the next boat and treat now while waiting.
Place the baby on the side, clear the airway, give oxygen if available, and check blood sugar.
Give midazolam IV/IM 1.5 mg (0.15 mg/kg, max 10 mg) or buccal/intranasal 2.9 mg (0.3 mg/kg, max 10 mg).
If midazolam is not available, give diazepam IV 2.0 mg (0.2 mg/kg, max 10 mg) or PR 2.9 mg (0.3 mg/kg, max 10 mg).
Watch the breathing after each dose and keep the baby on the side.

[guideline: DIARRHOEA p36] HOME MANAGEMENT - Give the child more fluids more often. Any locally available home fluid should be used e.g: thin soups from boiled vegetables (rice water, sweet potato water, banana water), green coconut water or cooled boiled water - Give child as much fluid as they will drink and after every watery stool - Continue giving the extra fluids until the diarrhoea stops - Give the child plenty of food to prevent undernutrition - Continue to breast feed frequently. - Give fresh fruit or mashed banana to provide potassium. - Give freshly prepared foods. Rice, sweet potato or taro mixed with vegetable and meat or fish are good. Cook and mash or grind food well - Encourage the child to eat; offer food at least 6 times a day - After the diarrhoea stops, give an extra meal each day for two weeks - Ask the mother to bring the child back for review if - Many watery stools or repeated vomitting - Very thirsty or inadequately drinking or eating - Fever and unwell - Blood in the stool - Symptom's persist greater than 2 weeks - Counsel family that due to inflammation of the gut, loose bowel motions may continue for up to 2 weeks however the diarrhoea should slowly improve. - If persistant, see prolonged diarrhoea (>14 days)

[guideline: MALARIA p53] INVESTIGATION - Malaria slide (MPS) OR Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) - Blood glucose MANAGEMENT - Consider malaria in any child with a fever. Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria

Girl 5 years, 17.3 kg, RDT positive for malaria. She had a fit at home this morning and now she is very sleepy, cannot wake properly for water. Skin and eyes look yellow. Next boat is tomorrow morning. What do I do now?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: MALARIA
---
Convulsion, lethargy and jaundice in a child with a positive RDT means severe malaria. Send her to hospital on the next boat, do not wait.
Before the boat: give artesunate 2.4 mg/kg intramuscularly (about 42 mg for 17.3 kg) if you have it and are trained.
Keep her warm, on the side, and give nothing by mouth while she is sleepy.
Check blood sugar if you can and treat low sugar as the manual says.
Write down the fit time and the RDT result and send the note with her.

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

Start ORS now if she can drink, small sips often, and keep breastfeeding or giving fluids.

Girl 8 years, about 27.9 kg. She has been coughing and now she is grunting and her nostrils are flaring. She is drowsy and will not take anything by mouth. No RDT and no ACT in the clinic. Boat only comes next week.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: PNEUMONIA
---
Grunting, nasal flaring and no oral intake are severe pneumonia signs, and drowsiness is a danger sign.
She needs hospital, so arrange the next boat and radio the hospital now.
While waiting, give amoxycillin 40 mg/kg: 1100 mg by mouth if she can swallow safely.
Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg (about 420 mg) for fever.
If she cannot swallow or gets worse, call the AHC by radio and keep her on her side.
